title: Azure Resource Hierarchy
description: Understand how Azure organizes resources using management groups, subscriptions, resource groups, and individual resources.

data.text: Azure uses a strict hierarchy to organize all resources. This hierarchy helps you manage access, billing, and policies across your entire cloud environment. Understanding it is essential before you start creating resources.
From top to bottom, the Azure management hierarchy has four main levels: management groups, subscriptions, resource groups, and resources.

data.title: Hierarchy Levels
items: **Management Groups** — The top level. Used to manage access, policies, and compliance across multiple subscriptions.
**Subscriptions** — A logical container for billing and access control. Every resource belongs to exactly one subscription.
**Resource Groups** — Containers that hold related resources for an application or solution. Resources in the same group can be managed, deployed, and monitored together.
**Resources** — Individual Azure services like virtual machines, storage accounts, or SQL databases.

data.caption: Azure resource hierarchy from top-level management down to individual resources
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[Management Group] --> B[Subscription 1]
    A --> C[Subscription 2]
    B --> D[Resource Group: Production]
    B --> E[Resource Group: Development]
    D --> F[Virtual Machine]
    D --> G[Storage Account]
    E --> H[Virtual Machine]
    E --> I[SQL Database]

data.text: The hierarchy controls how resources inherit settings. For example, if you apply a policy at the management group level, it applies to every subscription and resource beneath it. Similarly, if you give a user access to a resource group, they can manage all resources inside that group.

terms.definition: A top-level container that organizes subscriptions for governance and policy management.
A logical and billing boundary for Azure resources. Every resource belongs to one subscription.
A container that holds related Azure resources for an application or workload.
An individual Azure service instance, such as a virtual machine or database.

data.title: One Subscription, Many Groups
data.text: A single subscription can contain many resource groups. A resource group can contain many resources. But a resource belongs to exactly one resource group, and a resource group belongs to exactly one subscription.
Explore the Hierarchy with the CLI
Each level has its own command. Notice that management groups and subscriptions are account-level concepts, while resource groups and resources are scoped to a subscription.

data.title: List each level of the hierarchy
data.content: The output table makes the relationship easy to see; use `--output json` when a script needs to read ids.
data.code:
az account management-group list --output table
az account list --output table
az group list --output table
az resource list --resource-group rg-demo --output table

data.title: Scope a Bicep file to a resource group
data.content: The targetScope tells the deployment where the resources will be created. The same pattern works at subscription, management group, and tenant scope.

data.title: Inheritance is the point of the hierarchy
data.text: RBAC role assignments and Azure Policy assignments applied at a management group flow down to every subscription, resource group, and resource beneath it. A policy that denies public IP addresses at the management group level cannot be overridden in a child subscription. This is why platform teams put guardrails at the top and let application teams work inside them.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Azure uses a four-level hierarchy: management group, subscription, resource group, resource
Settings at higher levels flow down to lower levels
Resource groups are the main container you will work with as a developer
data.takeaway: The Azure hierarchy keeps your cloud environment organized and makes governance possible.
